pr_title: ARC: interrupt management fix for SMP case
pr_body:
**NOTE**: one part of the described issues is already fixed & merged as a separate PR #52387. The priority issue is still a thing and this PR can be used as a reference about how we can workaround this.
--------------------------


## issue description

In case of SMP system interrupt infrastructure implementation for ARC has serious design flaw.

We have per-core interrupt controllers private for each core. They are used to control interrupts - enable/disable, set priority. The IDU (interrupt distribution unit) is setup to distribute interrupts to different cores in the round-robin manner.

The irq management functions (`irq_enable`, `irq_disable`, `irq_is_enabled`) setup/check interrupt controller state only for the core where they are called. This cause inconsistency - we may have interrupt enabled on one core and disabled it on another. Such approach makes common interrupts unusable in case of SMP - there is no correct way to enable/disable interrupt line, we will lose some interrupts if we simple use `irq_enable` or we will get unexpected interrupts if we use `irq_disable`. See #31298 for example.

## reworked implementation description

We manage interrupts (enable/disable) with IDU instead of per-core interrupt controller for the common interrupts. The per-core interrupts enabling/disabling is still managed by per-core interrupt controller.

The interrupt priority can't be managed by IDU so we still control it with per-core interrupt controller. We setup interrupt priority at init stage. For that we collect interrupt priority of static interrupts in compile time. We don't support dynamic interrupts for the common interrupts for SMP systems for now.

We keep interrupt handling on all CPUs, and we do initial interrupt controller setup on all CPUs and enable round-robin interrupt distribution mode in IDU. However we move IDU setup from SoC code to generic ARC code.

NOTE: this patch doesn't include arc interrupts initialization optimization & cleanup (such as removing of excessive locking in core / IDU interrupts setup functions and implementation of proper *_nolock functions analogs). This will be done in separate PR.

Fixes: #31415
Fixes: #31298
pr_comments:
General principle is fine to fix the SMP interrupt management (for dynamic interrupts, some IPI would be required to set priorities, but I'm fine with this static solution).
See few additional comments inline.
@evgeniy-paltsev ok to remove the draft label? I think this is ready for broader review and merging now.

issue_context.title: [RFC] ARC: interrupt management rework
issue_context.body:
## Problem description

In case of SMP system interrupt infrastructure implementation for ARC has issues.

We have per-core interrupt controllers private for each core. We setup interrupt controller only on CPU0 and route all external interrupts to CPU0. 
That makes our SMP system not so symmetric, but things are getting worse when we start using dynamic interrupts - as when task which is enabling interrupt can be executed on CPU != 0, so we enable interrupt on, lets say, CPU1, however IDU will route interrupt on CPU0 for processing (where it is still disabled). See #31298 for example.
Quite similar situation with dynamic interrupt disabling is also possible.

As I understand the per-core private interrupts (like timer0/1 interrupts) are working now by lucky chance - as we have all interrupts enabled in per-core interrupt controller and we don't setup it for CPU != 0.


## How to fix - option 1:
We allow interrupt handling only on CPU0 (as we have it now)
We allow interrupt management function to be executed only on CPU0.

Pros:
- Easy to implement.

Cons:
- 'not so symmetric' SMP
- noticeably inconvenient for users if they use dynamic interrupts

Require clarifications:
- Is the chance that such 'not so symmetric' SMP implementation may cause performance degradation?


## How to fix - option 2:
We allow interrupt handling on all CPUs, so we do initial interrupt controller setup on all CPUs and enable round-robin interrupt distribution mode in IDU.
The dynamic interrupt enabling/disabling must be done on all CPUs which require invocations some code with ICI (inter-core-interrupts)

Pros:
- real SMP
- all interrupts can be dynamic, even per-core. But do we really need this?

Cons:
- simple function like enable_interrupt becomes quite heavy and requires inter-core-interrupts invocation.
- with ICI invocation it is really easy create new issues (which are badly reproducible and badly debuggable) in other corner cases.

Require clarifications:
- What would we break by adding ICI for interrupt management on per-cpu interrupt controllers?


## How to fix - option 3:
We allow interrupt handling on all CPUs, so we do initial interrupt controller setup on all CPUs and enable round-robin interrupt distribution mode in IDU.
We manage interrupts (enable/disable) with IDU instead of per-core interrupt controller.
The common interrupts can be software generated with CMD_IDU_GEN_CIRQ, so test for dynamic interrupts still can be implemented.

Pros:
- real SMP
- IDU is global, so we don't need inter-core-interrupts for interrupts management
- approach proven by Linux kernel

Cons:
- only common interrupts can be dynamic (do we really need dynamic per-core interrupts?)
- different interrupt controller used for UP and SMP

Require clarifications:
- what should we do with interrupt priority - it is still controlled by per-core interrupt controller? The Linux kernel uses single interrupt priority.
comments:
Few initial thoughts:

- reserving one core to handle all interrupts indeed sounds 'not so symmetric', but is a simple, predictable solution
- option 2 with round-robin distribution doesn't seem the best choice from performance (IPI overhead) and predictability/performance (a very frequently called interrupt would preferable run on the same core, with warm caches - though L1 will probably be replaced by other code, unless the CPU is idle.
- option 3 makes most sense to me, managing SMP interrupts at IDU level. Interrupt affinity could be controlled that way as well.
- besides external interrupts through IDU, timer interrupt(s) and other local interrupts (WDT, uDMA, etc.) that are per-CPU need to be considered as well

Maybe start with '1' and have a broader Zephyr discussion on handling SMP interrupts (incl. APIs for affinity etc.)?

I've investigated a bit about `arch_irq_{disable|enable}` usage. In `include/irq.h` we do define

```
#define irq_enable(irq) arch_irq_enable(irq)
#define irq_disable(irq) arch_irq_disable(irq)
```

And rest of the Zephyr code actively uses `irq_{disable|enable}`. So we can't simply restrict interrupt management function to be executed only on CPU0 as it will break drivers/subsystems. **IOW - option 1 is no go**.

As drivers/subsystems control external interrupts only the option 3 should be OK for them. However there is at least one place (`tests/kernel/context`) where we enable and disable ARC tick timer interrupt (IRQ_TIMER0). This corner case needs to be investigated as we can't control timer interrupt with IDU.

Thoughts about issue with interrupt priority in case of 'option 3':

We can't control interrupt priority with IDU so we have to configure interrupt priority via per-core interrupt controller.
Generally it should be OK as we need to do that only once - at the per-core interrupt controller init step.
There are several places where you can shoot in the leg, so the initialization needs to be done carefully. For example we need to enable round-robin interrupt distribution mode in IDU only after the interrupt controllers of each core are initialized.

The things are getting more complicated in case of dynamic interrupts as we can't configure interrupt priority at init step of the per-core interrupt controller. This means that we do configuration on each core in the moment of `irq_connect_dynamic` call. That obviously require ICI usage.

As of today dynamic interrupt subsystem has limitation:
> Removing or re-configuring a dynamic interrupt is currently unsupported.

so, most likely, the ICI usage shouldn't cause the problems
 * we do it once per interrupt - it shouldn't bring performance penalty
 * we do it on the interrupt disabled at the moment of configuration - there shouldn't be tricky synchronization issues

> So we can't simply restrict interrupt management function to be executed only on CPU0 as it will break drivers/subsystems. **IOW - option 1 is no go**.

Why not? it is 'just' that interrupt functions running on other cores would need to forward the request to CPU 0 with an IPI request (for external interrupts). Overhead of this would probably not be an issue, as irq_enable/disable() is typically used at (de)initialization only. But, it is more complex than you initially might have thought.

review_comments: Some comments why priority cannot be set here and is moved would be good (I don't really understand why it cannot be left here). Also, above comments might not be applicable at this location, when initialization is moved (not sure I understand the comment, or why it is a comment and not an assert).
Updated the comment for ARCH_IRQ_CONNECT, thanks!
Is testing via the get/set functions enough, or should there be some real interrupt triggering test to see if the get/set are implemented correctly?

Though for generic code the priority setting via the table is configurable, I see you make it the default for all ARC targets. Wouldn't it make sense to have it only enabled for SMP systems, and avoid the extra table? I didn't check the impact, but for systems with a large number of interrupts, wouldn't there be a size penalty for the tables?

Hi Ruud,

please don't forget that we are moving data from one place to another :)

I've done some measurements:

---
If we actually use interrupt lines (if we connect handlers to them) there is even a image size decrease:

Setup with IRQ used, hsdk board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=88), without changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            SRAM:       32728 B      1280 MB      0.00%
```

Setup with IRQ used, hsdk board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=88), with changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            SRAM:       32124 B      1280 MB      0.00%
```

Setup with IRQ used, nsim_hs board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=30), without changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            ICCM:        9896 B         1 MB      0.94%
            DCCM:        3672 B         1 MB      0.35%
```

Setup with IRQ used, nsim_hs board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=30), with changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            ICCM:        9780 B         1 MB      0.93%
            DCCM:        3672 B         1 MB      0.35%
```

----

However if we have a setup with a lot of interrupts which are **not used**, there is a small penalty:

Setup with IRQ unused, nsim_hs board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=30), without changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            ICCM:        9768 B         1 MB      0.93%
            DCCM:        3672 B         1 MB      0.35%
```

Setup with IRQ unused, nsim_hs board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=30), with changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            ICCM:        9776 B         1 MB      0.93%
            DCCM:        3672 B         1 MB      0.35%
```

Setup with IRQ unused, hsdk board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=88), without changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            SRAM:       32088 B      1280 MB      0.00%
```


Setup with IRQ unused, hsdk board (CONFIG_NUM_IRQS=88), with changes:
```
Memory region         Used Size  Region Size  %age Used
            SRAM:       32120 B      1280 MB      0.00%
```

The good news is that we can strip interrupt table (and interrupt priority table) if we don't use some of the interrupts.

There are another possible optimizations:
- we can disable interrupt priority table generation if we have only one interrupt priority level.
- we can introduce interrupt priority table packing (i.e on ARC we have 16 interrupt priorities levels, so is enough to have 4bits to store them)

However, I guess it would be better to have these optimizations in a separate PR.

Great to see the numbers, indeed the trade-off is between constant data and code. The increase without (many) ISRs installed is very small, let's avoid more #ifdef's. Other optimizations would (like you suggest) have more impact in that case.

Though for generic code the priority setting via the table is configurable, I see you make it the default for all ARC targets. Wouldn't it make sense to have it only enabled for SMP systems, and avoid the extra table? I didn't check the impact, but for systems with a large number of interrupts, wouldn't there be a size penalty for the tables?
